#6275. American Airlines Officially Discontinues Boeing 777-300ER Flagship First Sales

American Airlines stopped selling Flagship First on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet for travel on Thursday, ending the last long-haul international first-class product offered by a US airline. The cutoff removes eight seats from every aircraft in the 20-jet fleet. American disclosed the date on September 2, the day its first retrofitted 777-300ER entered revenue service between New York-JFK and Buenos Aires. Business class is now the highest cabin customers can buy on the type.

Flagship Suites will replace both former premium cabins. The retrofitted layout holds 70 lie-flat suites in a 1-2-1 arrangement, along with premium economy recliners and Main Cabin Extra seats, raising total capacity from 304 to 330. The aircraft, first delivered in 2012, was American’s only widebody with separate first and business cabins, and it serves long-haul routes from Miami, Dallas/Fort Worth, Los Angeles, New York-JFK, and Charlotte to cities including London, Tokyo, São Paulo, and Sydney.

Before the conversion, each aircraft carried eight Flagship First seats, 52 business seats, and 28 premium economy seats. The first class cabin included private airport check-in and a dedicated fine dining experience at select airports. Under the new layout, all 70 passengers in the forward cabin receive identical service, including priority check-in, security, boarding, and baggage handling. Eight of the suites carry the Flagship Suite Preferred label, with up to 19% more bed space and 42% more living area than the standard suite, and Afar reports that they inherit features once reserved for first class.

The wider refresh benefits other passengers as well. Every seat now has a personal entertainment screen, a feature the old main cabin lacked, and AAdvantage members receive free WiFi sponsored by AT&T, which was previously sold separately. Bluetooth connectivity, 4K screens, and power are standard throughout. American also expanded Flagship Dining access to all Flagship customers, and lounge access remains available where offered.

American is the last of the three largest network carriers to drop a separate international first class, following United and Delta, which gave up the cabin years ago. According to Fast Company & Inc., all three have judged a standalone first cabin no longer worth the floor space it occupies. The move has been tied to carriers chasing higher-spending travelers, according to KSL.

The seat math supports that reading. The Points Guy counted 60 lie-flat seats before the retrofit and 70 after, and premium economy grows from 28 to 44 seats. American says the result is more premium seats than any other US carrier operates on a single aircraft. United, the only other US operator of the 777-300ER, retrofitted its fleet in 2019 to hold up to 60 business class seats, leaving American with the larger premium cabin on the type.

The paradigm shift in premium air travel at AA.

Transcontinental Flagship First follows on March 28, 2027, with the cutoff tied to more Airbus A321XLR aircraft entering the fleet. The A321 Transcon subfleet, which serves only Boston, Los Angeles, New York, Orange County, and San Francisco, currently offers 10 first class and 20 business seats, and American has been converting those jets to a standard domestic first class layout. The A321XLR, by comparison, carries 20 Flagship Suites with 155 total seats.

On the widebody side, American plans to retrofit all 20 777-300ERs by the end of 2027. The first aircraft, registered N718AN, spent eight months out of service in Hong Kong for its interior work, an indication of the scale of the program. The sources reviewed do not say how aircraft awaiting retrofit will be configured or sold after November 19, so travelers booking in the near term may want to confirm the cabin on their specific flight. Flagship Suites already fly on the 787-9 and the A321XLR, so the 777-300ER conversion carries the brand across three fleets. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called the aircraft “the next evolution of premium travel at American”.

#6274. Sunrise Airways Launches New U.S. Service

Haiti’s Sunrise Airways this week launched a new route to the U.S. Northeast.

The carrier on Tuesday operated its inaugural flight between Cap-Haïtien and New York-JFK. Flights will operate twice per week going forward.

Sunrise is one of only two airlines currently connecting the U.S. and Haiti. It also serves Boston, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Miami from Cap-Haïtien.

American Airlines resumed service to the country earlier this month after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by rising gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince. It is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haïtien.

#6272. Why Long-Haul Flights Carry 3 Or 4 Pilots & How Airbus Wants To Cut Some To 2

Essentially, all commercial airliners in service today need two pilots: one captain and a first officer. These two have always been present on large transport aircraft, but airliners of the past also included a flight engineer, with earlier models even having a dedicated navigator and radio operator. However, as technology advanced and more aircraft functions were automated, manufacturers trimmed down flight crews until today, when most flights require only two pilots. Still, many widebody flights operate with three or four pilots, as one or two pilots may serve as a relief pilot.

This is done on long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights because crew rest regulations allow each pilot to work only a limited number of hours each day. The larger roster allows pilots to rotate throughout the flight, with one or two resting onboard. This arrangement ensures compliance with regulations and preserves safety, but it's also expensive. As such, some airlines and Airbus are looking to change it.

Exact practices vary by local regulations and sometimes by standard airline operating procedures. Generally, however, the rule of thumb is that any flight over eight hours requires a third pilot to be rostered, while flights scheduled to exceed 12 hours must be staffed with four pilots. All crew members will be present in the flight deck during critical phases of flight.

Meanwhile, during cruise, they will rotate among each other so that two crew members are flying while the third (and fourth, if applicable) are resting. Some carriers will roster the relief pilot as either another first officer or captain, while others may specifically roster 'second officers' (also known as cruise pilots) who do not perform takeoffs or landings.

On the world's longest flights, carriers will typically staff flights with two of their most senior captains and two of their most senior first officers, while carriers that roster second officers will not schedule them on their longest services. The actual onboard rest schedule is typically determined by the pilots themselves, developed in such a way to ensure compliance with the airline's home regulator. Onboard, most modern widebody aircraft are equipped with crew rest pods located either above or below the passenger cabin, featuring two beds as well as a seat. These are often, but not always, separate from the flight attendant crew rest area, while aircraft that do not include a dedicated rest area instead have blocked business class seats for pilots.

Most airline pilots are paid by the hour, which means that crew costs increase the longer a flight is. In addition, longer services require an extra pilot or two, which can nearly double pilot salary costs on an ultra-long-haul service. When taking into account that most long-haul flights are performed by widebody aircraft, this further increases crew costs.

After all, widebodies pay more than a narrowbody aircraft type, resulting in extremely high labor costs for a 12, 13, or 15-hour flight using large twin-aisle jets. Long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights are quite challenging economically due to added fuel costs, overflight fees, and staffing costs. Augmented crews typically no longer require blocked seats due to the widespread use of underfloor or crown-area rest pods.

However, the costs of rostering a captain and three first officers or two captains and two first officers on their own are immense. This is especially true when considering that pilots who regularly operate ultra-long-haul services are typically an airline's most senior and best-paid crew members. The airline industry is infamously cost-sensitive, and ultra-long-haul flights are the most difficult for an airline to make money on.

This is despite the revenue premium that they typically command. Airlines, already constantly hunting for ways to reduce operating costs, have also been turning to pilots for more savings, particularly on widebody ultra-long-haul flights. For its part, Airbus has been working on systems to eliminate the need for augmented crews on the A350, which includes the ability to cruise with just one crew member at the controls.

Modern airliners are incredibly automated, but pilots remain fully responsible for every decision during a flight. What do they actually do?

Airbus has been working on developing systems to enable extended Minimum Crew Operations (eMCO) for the A350. With this system, the aircraft still requires two pilots for takeoffs and landings, but one crew member would rest during cruise while the other would be present at the controls. The two would then rotate throughout the flight, with only one pilot actively flying at a time.

Airbus's role would be to redesign cockpit displays and modify systems to reduce workload on the pilot. It has been working with airlines such as Cathay Pacific and Lufthansa to evaluate the feasibility of eMCO, while also working with EASA to assess whether the concept compromises safety.

The agency launched a proposal in 2022, which was sent to ICAO, and aimed to potentially transition to eMCO operations as early as 2027. This could allow airlines to significantly cut crew costs for long-haul flights while also reducing the impact of the widely reported pilot shortage. Airbus has been discussing with customers implementing this potential new feature throughout the A350 family.

It has also been looking at potentially implementing the technology in the upcoming A350F, which is set to enter service in 2027. While Airbus has been pushing for the development of eMCO procedures, Boeing has stated that the technology isn't yet in place for single-pilot cruise operations to be executed safely. What's more, while there was momentum for Airbus's eMCO initiative, this has since faded.

In February 2026, the US Congress passed a new law requiring two pilots to be present at all times in the flight deck on all commercial airline flights. While this was previously enforced by FAA regulations, the new legislation codifies this into law, essentially closing any pathways for airlines and manufacturers to push for single-pilot operations.

While it wouldn't be impossible for this law to be undone, it's much more difficult to change the law than to amend FAA regulations. EASA has paused and shelved its research on eMCO and single-pilot operations, concluding that implementing such practices would reduce safety.

The regulator was particularly concerned about fatigue management, meeting a pilot's physiological needs, and cross-checking between crew members. As such, it ruled out any regulatory changes in the near future. Instead, the focus is on improving cockpit technologies rather than reducing the number of pilots in the flight deck.

While it's often been discussed that airline flight crews have shrunk throughout history, what is often overlooked is that not everyone performs the same function. Flight engineers, navigators, and radio operators all served distinct roles, while there were always two pilots who primarily flew the aircraft. The functions formerly handled by flight engineers, navigators, and radio operators have either been automated or are now handled by the pilots.

This kind of aircraft requires some creative crew management.

Regulators have rejected single-pilot operations on commercial transport aircraft. EASA has shelved any plans to operate airliners with one pilot at any time, while the US has prohibited this by law. What's more, existing single-pilot aircraft remain under scrutiny, as the FAA has recently rescinded single-pilot operation exemptions for several Cessna Citation models.

This was due to increased accident rates, reportedly double compared with two-pilot flights, along with widespread compliance failures. At the same time, pilots are expensive, and the airline industry is particularly cost-sensitive, which makes developments that cut down on crew costs quite lucrative to airlines. In addition to initiatives like Airbus's work on eMCO for the A350, Merlin is working on developing new AI-assisted copilot systems that could be installed on essentially any large airliner. While these systems are meant to assist pilots at first, the long-term goal is to enable single-pilot or fully autonomous operations.

The burden on Airbus or Merlin is to prove that their proposals materially enhance safety compared to today's system of mandating at least two pilots during a flight. Thus far, they have failed to prove this, which means that these systems cannot be implemented in their intended form in the near future. What will happen in the distant future is unclear, but regulators have a responsibility to maintain and enhance safety in aviation, first and foremost.

#6269. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6268. JetBlue Adds New Destination in Latin America, Caribbean Expansion

JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

On Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

JetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline said.

“We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, said in a news release. “With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”

American has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently launched service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

Dallas has finally gained scheduled flight operations from the city's third airport, Dallas McKinney National Airport (DTX). The airport is located to the north of the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex and has already become Avelo Airlines' second busiest airport in its network.

For ultra-low-cost carrier Avelo, the first route for the airline from McKinney was nonstop to Fort Myers in Florida. The service departed last Wednesday and was quickly followed by Orlando and Las Vegas as the airline's first three domestic services. More flights were added on November 19, with Fort Lauderdale and Tampa taking flight.

Following the opening of the airport's new terminal and facilities, Avelo has become the first scheduled operator at the airport. The airport was the first in Texas to be granted an FAA Part 139 Airport Operating Certificate since 2005. Avelo picked McKinney to serve the fast-growing suburbs of North Texas, and provides a smaller-airport alternative when compared to the much busier Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW) and Dallas-Love Field (DAL).

McKinney's operational structure fits in well with Avelo's low-cost structure, and the airline is primarily focusing on leisure routes, such as Nevada and Florida.

With the first three routes already operating, two more beginning on November 19, and six more to be added before Christmas, McKinney's total network is 11 nonstop destinations. This has helped the airport become the airline's second-largest airport just weeks after opening (more on that in the next section). Below are the details of the airline's first three services to Fort Myers, Las Vegas, and Orlando:

Data from Cirium indicates that in the first quarter of 2027, McKinney will become the airline's second-busiest airport by total flight departures. This would see McKinney overtake Wilmington (ILM) in Delaware and sit behind the region's busiest airport, Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN), in Connecticut.

McKinney's new passenger terminal has seen the launch of its first commercial flights by Avelo, marking the latest chapter for the airport after 40 years as a facility primarily used for general aviation. The airport is owned by the City of McKinney and is home to many business aircraft and fleets for global companies, like Texas Instruments and Toyota Motor Corporation.

In 2025, the city approved the construction of the new commercial passenger terminal for $72 million. This has now lured in Avelo as the first operator at the airport. Avelo remains the only airline to announce flights from the airport, with hometown Dallas airline Southwest already signaling it has no immediate interest in serving the airport as the 'numbers don't stack up'.

Avelo will launch five routes from McKinney, giving Dallas a third commercial airport.

On November 19, McKinney gained two more nonstop domestic flights from Avelo, as Fort Lauderdale and Tampa began regular scheduled services. The airline will operate the route to Fort Lauderdale up to six times weekly, while Tampa sees a four-weekly rotation.

Additional flights are set to begin in December, with Atlanta, Denver, and Sarasota scheduled to all commence on December 16. This will be the airline's biggest one-day expansion from McKinney, with three new services all beginning on the same day.

The next day will be just as busy, as December 17 sees new services to Nashville (BNA), New Orleans (MSY), and West Palm Beach These services will all run twice weekly.

Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners. Now, just in time for the holiday shopping season, Rove has launched personalized shopping offers that let members earn up to 25 Rove miles per dollar on select purchases. The program has also expanded its in-store shopping offers.

Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card. TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Rove miles at 2.05 cents apiece, so earning 25 Rove miles per dollar could yield rewards of up to 51.25 cents per dollar spent.

Here's what you should know about Rove's new offerings.

Not a Rove member yet? The program is free to join, and you can score 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link.

Rove members already know they can navigate to the shopping tab on the Rove website or app and see featured offers or search for a specific merchant.

Now, Rove members who link and connect an eligible payment card can access personalized offers in the For You section of Rove's website and app.

When a personalized offer has a higher earning rate than Rove's standard offer, you'll see both rates displayed. Since these offers are personalized, the available merchants and earning rates may vary by member. Plus, a Rove spokesperson told TPG that Rove refreshes its offers each week, so you may see new or different offers the next time you check.

You'll need to activate each offer before making a qualifying purchase. Click the plus button to activate, and then check the circle that replaces the plus after activation to see how long you have to use the offer.

Be sure to review each offer's terms before purchasing, including where the offer is valid, when it expires and whether any spending limits or purchase exclusions apply.

By reviewing the Hyatt House and Hyatt Studios offer I enrolled in, I found it is only valid for stays within the U.S. This is too bad, as I was excited to use it for an upcoming Hyatt House stay in Canada until I read its terms.

Finally, it's worth noting that neither TPG's Lyndsey Matthews nor I saw any offers in our For You sections for 25 miles per dollar spent. Instead, 15 miles per dollar spent on a new Sam's Club membership purchase is the best offer either of us found in our accounts.

Related: Why the holiday season is the best time to start earning points and miles

Rove initially introduced in-store card-linked offers in August. It now says members can earn miles on qualifying purchases at hundreds of participating physical retailers.

To earn Rove miles on an in-store purchase, link an eligible card to Rove and review the merchant's offer before making a purchase. Activate the offer first if required, then use your linked card to make a qualifying purchase. Rove says transactions are automatically tracked after the charge clears and that miles typically post within seven days.

Related: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season

Rove's personalized offers could be a lucrative way to earn transferable rewards on purchases you already planned to make, especially when targeted rates reach 25 miles per dollar.

However, offers and earning rates will vary by member, so check the For You section and review the activation and purchase requirements before shopping. You should also compare Rove's rate with other shopping portals and check for card-linked merchant offers you may be able to stack with your purchase.

#6265. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

I use ChatGPT most days and am just getting started with using Instinct AI via WhatsApp. And I'm increasingly using AI to plan and improve my travels. For example, I frequently ask ChatGPT to plan walking tours in new destinations, use Instinct to find stores selling specific items and even tried connecting Gondola to ChatGPT for more personalized travel advice.

But as AI tools become increasingly capable of booking trips and managing accounts on your behalf, airlines and banks are becoming increasingly concerned about how consumers use them. For example, United Airlines recently announced restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, while Bank of America warned customers against sharing their banking passwords with AI assistants.

These developments don't mean you should stop using AI to plan your travels. But they highlight why it's important to understand — and thoughtfully consider — what information you're sharing, what you're allowing AI to do and when you should verify its recommendations.

Before we dive into the dos and don'ts, let's discuss how consumers are using AI for travel. Most usage falls into one of three categories:

Each of these types of AI usage carries different risks. So, especially as AI agents become more capable, it's important to understand the risks you're taking when using them.

Related: How AI is transforming the future of travel

One way travelers can use AI is to help them research and plan trips. I've used AI to research and plan trips with extended family to both Iceland and Venice. And I use AI most days to help me plan walking routes in new cities, decipher restaurant menus and figure out how to operate appliances in Airbnbs.

While researching and planning travel, you can also use AI to:

Besides the time you can save and the experiences you can discover, the best part of using AI to research and plan your travels is that you can often provide enough context to help the AI improve its recommendations without sharing unnecessary personal information. As such, using AI to plan and research your travels is often relatively low-risk.

Related: Can Hilton’s new AI planning tool help you find the perfect hotel? We put it to the test

You can also use AI to help you with your points and miles. For example, AI can suggest ways to stack earnings and help you decide the best card to use before you make a purchase. However, you have to provide the AI with the proper context, such as the merchant you want to buy from, whether you want to prioritize having extended warranty protection, whether you're working toward any minimum spending requirements and which cards you currently have in your wallet.

AI could also help you compare cards when you're ready to open a new card. And it can also help you with many of the calculations travelers often struggle with, such as comparing cash versus points bookings (you can also use TPG's calculator for this), calculating redemption values, evaluating whether transferring points makes sense and assessing elite status benefits.

Best of all, it can do all these tasks without needing access to your accounts. Sure, the more information you give the AI agent, the more accurate and relevant its responses may be. But you don't need to give an AI agent access to your accounts for it to compare properties at your desired destination, calculate whether it's better to redeem 25,000 Hyatt points or pay $600, or compare the perks of using two different cards for a purchase.

Related: The 9 best rewards credit cards to add to your wallet

Even as many travelers start to use AI for more travel decisions and planning, it's important to fact-check or verify anything an AI agent tells you that you plan to rely on.

Sure, it doesn't really matter if ChatGPT gets a few details about landmarks incorrect during a walking tour I asked it to plan. And it's only a minor inconvenience if it sends me to a closed restaurant or suggests I get off at a slightly farther away bus stop.

But many travel decisions do matter and should be verified. For example, verify driving routes and travel times, entry requirements and whether a hotel offers the amenities you need. I also recommend ensuring that any redemption rates or other calculations pass the "sniff test" and appear correct. And if you ask an AI agent to find sweet spots in a specific loyalty program, be sure to fact-check that the sweet spots still exist at the stated rates and that you can find availability on at least some dates.

Also keep in mind that AI may give you overly conservative advice. For example, it will often recommend arriving at the airport three to four hours before your flight even when the bag drop counter doesn't open until two hours before departure. So, double-check any information that you'd be upset if it were incorrect.

Although sharing information with AI can help you get more personalized advice, you should carefully consider what to share. In particular, avoid sharing passwords, security codes, full credit card numbers and other sensitive information with AI tools.

Bank of America recently warned customers not to share their banking usernames or passwords with AI assistants, noting that customers could be responsible for certain activity resulting from that access. This is good advice for your loyalty accounts, too.

However, you don't necessarily need to avoid sharing any personal information with AI agents. For example, uploading a flight itinerary or hotel reservation could help an AI assistant plan your travels. Consider removing unnecessary details, such as confirmation numbers, account numbers and other identifying information, before uploading documents.

If you've already shared a password with an AI tool, change it immediately and review your account for unauthorized activity.

Related: Why one of the best tools for maximizing rewards is ... a password manager?

As AI agents become more capable, you may be tempted to let them access your loyalty and banking accounts to search for award availability, manage reservations or even book travel on your behalf. But just because an AI agent can access an account doesn't mean the account's provider allows it.

For example, United Airlines recently announced restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents accessing its systems, citing concerns about unauthorized purchases, MileagePlus redemptions and automated check-in. Meanwhile, American Airlines explicitly prohibits "automated re-shopping," and Marriott prohibits automated tools from monitoring or retrieving website information without written permission.

Likewise, some financial institutions restrict how third-party tools can access customer accounts. For example, Chase updated its digital services agreement last month to prohibit third parties, including AI agents, from using customers' login credentials to access accounts.

However, this doesn't mean all AI integrations are prohibited. Some companies allow customers to connect their accounts to approved third-party services through secure connections that don't require sharing passwords.

So, before connecting an AI agent to your travel or financial accounts, check whether the company permits the integration. And even if an integration is authorized, understand what information the AI tool can access, what actions it can take and how to revoke access if you change your mind.

As I was using Instinct AI to research clothing I needed to buy during a trip, its responses kept saying "Nothing has been ordered." This was reassuring on one hand, but I also found myself thinking, "I definitely don't want it ordering anything without my approval."

In the travel realm, actions an AI agent might take without your approval could include:

In short, it's a good idea to keep yourself in the loop. Even if you decide to use an AI agent or connection to make purchases or change reservations, you should require it to explicitly get approval from you each time.

That said, I generally prefer that the AI agent flag potential price drops or award availability for me. Then I verify the information it has told me, and consider whether to act on it.

Related: These new tools will track your flights and get you refunds if the price drops

For each AI tool you use, take the time to understand how the company collects, stores and uses your data. After all, you may be sharing more information than you realize, especially if you're uploading documents or connecting third-party accounts.

For example, some AI services may use your conversations to train or improve their models. Others may retain information even after you delete a conversation. And if you're using an AI tool through another platform, such as WhatsApp, or connecting a third-party service, multiple companies may have access to your information.

AI tools can be incredibly useful for planning trips, maximizing points and miles, and making travel easier. I use them frequently and expect I'll continue finding more ways to incorporate them into my travels.

But as AI tools become more capable, it's increasingly important to understand their limitations and the risks of sharing information or granting them access to your accounts.

My advice is to start with relatively low-risk tasks, such as researching destinations and comparing redemption options. Then, as you become more comfortable with AI tools, consider whether you're willing to share more information or allow them to take actions on your behalf. Just be sure to understand what you're authorizing and maintain control over your accounts and reservations.

#6262. 2 Virgin Australia Pilots Admit They’re Too Tired To Continue Flying, Immediately Offloaded

Two Virgin Australia pilots declared themselves unfit to continue flying after fatigue set in during a domestic flight from Melbourne Airport (MEL) to Adelaide Airport (ADL) on Wednesday. Both crew members requested to be stood down upon reaching their destination. The aircraft landed safely at Adelaide Airport, after which the pilots were immediately removed from further flying duties.

The incident highlights the importance of fatigue management in commercial aviation, where pilots must recognize when tiredness could compromise their ability to operate an aircraft safely. Although the flight itself was completed without incident, the decision to remove both pilots raises broader questions about crew scheduling, rest periods, and the challenges of managing fatigue across Australia's airline industry. Virgin Australia's response also shows why self-reporting remains essential to aviation safety.

According to AIRLIVE, the incident occurred aboard VA219 on Wednesday morning. The Boeing 737-800, registered VH-VUX, was operating a domestic service between Melbourne and Adelaide when both pilots reported fatigue. Rather than continue their planned duties, the flight crew requested to be stood down at their next destination.

The aircraft continued to Adelaide and completed its journey safely, touching down at 11:05 local time. The flight had departed Melbourne about an hour earlier, following the aircraft's previous operation of flight VA814 from Sydney to Melbourne earlier that morning. Once in Adelaide, both pilots were immediately offloaded, preventing them from operating any subsequent flight sectors until they were considered fit to return to duty.

The decision followed Virgin Australia's fatigue risk management procedures, which allow pilots to report when tiredness affects their ability to perform their responsibilities safely. Importantly, declaring oneself unfit to fly is not an admission of wrongdoing. It is a safety measure designed to prevent potentially impaired crew members from continuing operations.

This is not the first time fatigue management has attracted attention at Virgin Australia. In May 2024, The Guardian reported that senior pilots had raised concerns about the airline's rostering arrangements, arguing that demanding schedules were contributing to fatigue across the pilot workforce. Correspondence reviewed by the newspaper highlighted concerns about consecutive long duty days, sometimes lasting 11–12 hours, followed by the minimum 12-hour rest period permitted under the applicable rules.

The pilots also questioned the airline's rostering software and its ability to accommodate operational realities, particularly when flights were delayed. Virgin Australia responded at the time by saying it operated under a robust fatigue management system approved by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). The airline also highlighted that its pilots received 156 rostered days off annually. Although those earlier concerns do not establish the cause of the November 2026 report, they illustrate how crew scheduling and fatigue have remained important topics within the airline.

Fatigue is also a concern beyond the flight deck. Last month, ABC News reported on an Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation into a taxiway incident at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) involving Virgin Australia flight 1589 and Qantas flight 420. An air traffic controller working during the incident had a high predicted fatigue risk after being rostered to finish at 8:50 PM and return to duty at 5:30 AM the following morning. The ATSB stressed that a high predicted fatigue level does not necessarily mean an individual is actually fatigued. Nevertheless, the case demonstrates how demanding schedules can affect safety-critical aviation personnel across different operational environments.

While the aircraft involved landed safely at its planned destination, it is yet to return to service.

Fatigue can significantly affect a pilot's concentration, reaction time, memory, and decision-making under pressure. According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), tiredness can reduce the ability to perform tasks requiring manual coordination, vigilance, and higher-level cognitive processing. These effects can develop after a single demanding period or accumulate over several days of insufficient rest.

The consequences can be particularly serious in commercial aviation, where pilots must continuously monitor aircraft systems, communicate with air traffic control, assess changing weather conditions, and respond to unexpected situations. Even experienced flight crew members are not immune to these effects. The FAA also notes that coffee, medication, motivation, and willpower cannot overcome fatigue; adequate sleep remains the most effective solution.

Virgin Australia's decision to remove both pilots from further duties should be viewed positively. Allowing fatigued crew members to keep flying just to avoid disruption would create an unnecessary safety risk for passengers, other crew members, and everyone involved in the operation. While replacing pilots can create scheduling complications and potentially delay subsequent services, those considerations must remain secondary to operational safety.

This incident demonstrates an important principle of commercial aviation: a flight is only safe when its crew members are fit to perform their duties. By allowing both pilots to report their condition and immediately standing them down after arrival, Virgin Australia followed the appropriate safety-first approach.

#6261. Southwest Signs Interline Deal With French Bee

Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

It’s the end of an era at American Airlines.

This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.

We’ve been talking for years about American’s plans to retire its international-style first-class product.

The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.

But there’s at least a little nostalgia in bidding farewell to a cabin that, for many years, was billed as American’s most exclusive.

American was the last U.S. airline that claimed to offer a standalone, international first-class product.

Across the global airline industry, many carriers sunset long-haul first-class years ago, choosing to instead offer more — and improved — business-class seats, which take up less space and are considered more profitable.

For years, Delta Air Lines’ Delta One business-class suites have been its premier long-haul offering.

United Airlines bid farewell to international first class in 2018 when it pivoted to Polaris business class.

That left American’s Flagship First as a relic, of sorts, in the U.S. airline industry — and even on its own planes.

In recent years, you could only find the cabin on two fleet types American operated: its Boeing 777-300ER, which offered eight of the pods up front in their own dedicated cabin.

Plus, AA still (for now) offers Flagship First on its three-cabin Airbus A321T, which has been a fixture on lucrative coast-to-coast routes like New York to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

But soon, it will be a thing of the past on both planes.

American is retrofitting its larger 777s, ditching first-class in favor of 70 all-new Flagship Suites in business-class — along with the biggest premium economy cabin it’s ever offered.

Related: This is now American Airlines' most premium plane: Here's what it's like on board

On domestic routes, the A321T will actually keep flying with Flagship First through March 28.

But after that, AA will stop selling the Flagship First cabin on the A321T configuration, which is eventually going away as American flexes in its new A321XLR planes fully onto its top cross-country flights.

In a lot of ways, American ditching Flagship First is a positive (and arguably overdue) transition for flyers.

It’ll give passengers more lie-flat seats to pick from, whether they’re paying cash, using AAdvantage miles or using a systemwide upgrade.

Also — while those Flagship First seats were really spacious and comfortable, many would say that American's new business-class product is a major upgrade from what it previously offered in that cabin.

On some planes, that even includes extra-spacious Flagship Suites Preferred in the front and bulkhead rows of some planes, which offer a lot more space.

Value check: Is it worth buying up to American Airlines' new business-class Flagship Suite Preferred?

Beyond the aircraft, American also plans to still offer many of the same amenities for business-class that first-class passengers historically enjoyed.

For instance, its Flagship business-class tickets get access to its premium lounges. Passengers traveling in Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus on qualifying international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes will also be able to have a meal in its exclusive restaurant-style dining rooms in Dallas, Los Angeles and Miami.

The experience is available on a space-available basis.

So, in some ways, you could argue the end of Flagship First is more symbolic than anything.

But for some AA loyalists, it's still a little bittersweet.

TPG’s Clint Henderson is our resident Flagship First enthusiast, having flown the cabin on dozens of occasions.

"The service in first class wasn't particularly differentiated, but I still liked a few of the special touches," he said, pointing to the additional soup course and appetizer, along with a handful of elevated amenities.

He especially appreciated the “La-Z-Boy-style” seats at the front of American’s 777s, which could lie flat or swivel and turn into an “office in the sky.”

“While these cabins are definitely showing their age,” Henderson added, “I’m sad to see it go.”

While Flagship First is technically going away as an official cabin on international service, the seats themselves won't disappear overnight.

So far, American has only retrofitted one of its 20 Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the seats. That means a handful of jets with the old first-class seats will still be flying around well into 2027.

Going forward, the former Flagship First seats on those planes will be marketed as business-class. They won’t come with the full first-class service, but you’ll still get the elevated seat.

#6258. Report: Lufthansa to Cut 1,000 Jobs

Lufthansa Group plans to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

Company leaders said their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

“The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

#6257. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6256. Flexibility: How Flight Attendants Can Be Displaced From Their Schedule With Little Notice

Flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does. This guide will take a closer look at how it all works, when things change at the last minute, and what can happen to a flight attendant's schedule.

In the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input. It's all down to the airlines' operations teams and aviation regulators when it comes to how our schedules can change. Of course, flexibility is key, and things can happen unexpectedly, but that's all part of the fun of being a flight attendant or cabin crew.

When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely. One older contract, filed with the SEC, pays them for whichever is greater: the original assignment or the new one. Many US airline contracts call this "pay protection." This is a contractual rule that keeps a flight attendant's scheduled pay credit safe when flights change, get canceled, or get delayed through no fault of their own.

If the trip or a leg of the sequence is canceled, union collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) typically guarantee that they still get paid for the original scheduled value or the new assigned trip, whichever is greater. If crew scheduling alters the route or equipment after a disruption, pay protection ensures that they do not lose money if the new assignment ends up paying less than what was originally on the line.

Alaska Airlines' current agreement, for example, can remove a flight attendant from an assignment with pay protection and fly them home as a passenger; this is called deadheading. Under the 2025-2028 Collective Bargaining Agreement between Alaska Airlines and the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, line-holding flight attendants receive 150% pay on top of strong base trip protection when crew scheduling reassigns or reroutes a sequence. If a crew member is assigned to four or more legs over the original sequence, pay is 200%.

Trip displacement occurs when a crew member is involuntarily removed from a scheduled flight pairing or stranded away from their planned itinerary. This could be due to operational needs, regulatory limits, or personnel bumps; it is not a personal absence from duty. It can vary from airline to airline in the US, and union contracts may vary. At carriers without union contracts, such as Delta Air Lines, displaced flight attendants often do not receive automatic pay protection and must choose between sitting on-call availability or taking a lesser payment.

A flight attendant can also be bumped from a trip that they bid for. They can be displaced from trips to make room for training or for new hires' supervised flights, which are called operating experience. A flight attendant can be pulled from a trip so a supervisor, for example, can occupy that position for qualification or observation. In those cases, the displaced flight attendant gets a similar trip or is released from duty for the rest of the trip.

Frontier Airlines' 2019 contract requires at least 24 hours' notice before a flight attendant is displaced, and pays them for the trip they lost. Depending on the contract, crew scheduling may have a specific window (often matching the original trip's footprint) to assign replacement flights. If the airline does not reassign the flight attendant within those rules, the crew member is released with pay.

There is no such thing as 9 to 5 work here.

The one thing that most often catches US flight attendants off guard is the junior assignment, sometimes called junior availability or JA. This is a last-resort scheduling measure where an airline forces the most junior legal flight attendant to work a flight during their scheduled day off or open time because all reserve crews have been exhausted. This prevents cancellations or other disruptions when the reserve pool runs out, and it typically falls on the most junior available flight attendant.

This is used in cases such as major weather disruptions, holiday travel spikes, or high sick-call volume, after all on-call reserve flight attendants have already been assigned. Airlines assign these open trips starting from the absolute bottom of the seniority list at that base and working upward until the flight is covered. However, the new trip cannot violate mandatory rest requirements or maximum duty limits. This will also attract a premium payment, and the airline has to restore any lost days off.

Contracts usually limit how often junior assignments can happen. PSA Airlines' contract caps it at three days a month and bars assignments that are more than 24 hours in advance, while Silver Airways' contract limits it to twice a month. They also usually pay at a premium rate of 150% at Silver Airways and PSA Airlines, and 2.5 times the trip rate under Alaska Airlines' 2025–2028 contract. Silver Airways closed down in June 2025.

At some airlines, flight attendants who are already on duty at the airport, such as those arriving, checking in, or waiting in between flights, can be drafted onto another flight when time is critical, or the reserve pool is empty. Therefore, their entire schedule can change if a new trip is added or removed. Usually, crew scheduling tries not to disrupt the schedule too much and swaps them with a trip with similar timing, but of course, this is not always possible.

Flight attendants on reserve or standby are usually more junior crew with low seniority, are on call, and can be given trips with little notice. Many US-based crew start out on reserve and may do so for the first few years. At American Airlines, for example, flight attendants are on reserve for the first year and then move to one month on reserve, one month off reserve until year five, when it moves to one month on reserve and three months off according to their APFA contract.

At Delta Air Lines, junior flight attendants bid on a line and do not have to complete a full month on reserve. Instead, they have six 'A' days a month, where they are on call. If a Delta flight attendant's trip is canceled or removed, they only keep their pay if they convert to availability. Delta's order of assignment places displaced lineholders on availability ahead of A-Day reserves, and management holds broader discretion to modify trips during irregular operations.

United Airlines has reportedly terminated several senior flight attendants following an internal investigation into trip trading.

Airlines in the rest of the world rarely have union agreements, and schedules are set by the operations or crew scheduling department. Rosters are scheduled four to six weeks in advance in accordance with duty time regulations, so you know what your trips will be and your days off, if all goes to plan. Long-haul rosters don't change much, but short-haul rosters are more likely to change. There is no bidding for trips, although crew can sometimes request one or two trips a month; it is rare that they are given. Part-time work is very rare.

In addition, every crew member has some standby days, usually three or four per month, when you are on call to cover a trip at short notice because a flight attendant calls in sick or misses a trip. These are periods of around six to eight hours, and you would hope to be called at the beginning, not the end, of the shift. This can be at base, at the airport, or home standby; it varies by airline. Standby isn't just given to junior cabin crew; everyone has to do it, although seniority remains important throughout your career.

Some airlines also have available days that are filled 12 to 24 hours in advance; you could get a trip, standby duty, or be stood down, and then it becomes a day off. If a change is made to your schedule by operations, it shows up on your roster, and that's it; you do the trip. There is no payment protection pay, sit pay, or any extra payments for schedule changes. Rosters are more likely to change at the last minute due to being called out on standby duty or if a flight is delayed and doesn't allow enough rest, but it is more likely on a short-haul or mixed-fleet roster.

Every contract is different, so the rules, limits, and premium pay vary widely by airline and by where you are working. Large international airlines in Europe and the UK are not heavily unionized like those in the US, and they have no influence on your schedule or what you actually earn; that is up to the airline itself. In the Middle East, there are no unions.

The contracts noted here are for comparison to show how contracts have changed in recent years and are for reference only; not all the airlines still exist, and some may have merged. American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Southwest Airlines contracts have all changed significantly in recent years, affecting how flight attendants are scheduled and paid. Delta's flight attendants are not unionized, so their scheduling rules come from company policy rather than a contract.

Terminology used by airlines can also be different. In the UK, Europe, and the Middle East, instead of reserve, we have standby, and instead of operating experience for junior flight attendants, we have supernumerary flights. We do not have "junior assignment," "junior availability," "drafting," "reassignment," and "displacement," which can all mean slightly different things depending on the contract. Although it's the same job with the same rules, the terminology, scheduling system, and pay are very different.

#6255. American Plans Return to Israel, Partners With Israir

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

Israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

American also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. New York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

#6254. American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

“He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

“For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

#6251. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.
