#6180. American Airlines Says Operations Chief David Seymour Will Retire — With Dismissal-Style Severance

American Airlines chief operating officer David Seymour is leaving the job December 31. CEO Robert Isom calls it a retirement. The agreement American signed with Seymour gives him severance on terms normally reserved for dismissal without cause or resignation for good reason. American’s last proxy put the cash severance alone at $2,750,625 for a hypothetical departure on December 31, 2025, with total value over $7 million. The airline hasn’t disclosed the final amount for this exit. [T]he Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023

[T]he Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023

JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson takes over January 1, reporting directly to Isom. He’s the executive I flagged as Seymour’s likely successor in August, when American handed him much of the job.

Aviation watchdog JonNYC shared Isom’s message to employees. Isom thanks Seymour for his friendship and his work bringing US Airways and American together. Before joining America West in 1999, Seymour led a platoon in the 82nd Airborne. Just last month he went back to West Point and Fort Bragg with Medal of Honor recipients to meet the cadets and soldiers who followed him there.

AA pic.twitter.com/9919XVOKrW — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 20, 2026

Under Seymour’s contract, cash severance is 18 months of salary plus a year and a half of target bonus. He also gets money for 18 months of health premiums, and his stock can keep vesting during those 18 months. Between cash, stock, health premiums and flight benefits he’d already earned, American’s illustration in its latest proxy came to $7.13 million. Separately, Seymour remains eligible for his 2026 annual bonus. His advisory job pays $25,000 a month for up to three months ($75,000), plus executive benefits. His contract calculates severance using pay immediately before termination. Seymour has to sign a release and honor his existing restrictions, and American says it’ll file the full transition letter with its annual report. Those flight benefits include lifetime confirmed personal travel in any cabin for Seymour and his immediate family, Admirals Club access and another 12 confirmed roundtrips a year for friends and other relatives. The Handoff Started In August When American put Heather Garboden in charge of the customer experience, they gave her two bosses. She was supposed to persuade customers to pay more to fly American while reporting both to commercial and to the executive responsible for getting flights off the gate on time. When a pilot asked Seymour in 2022 what American was doing about poor customer satisfaction, his answer was “I think we’re on a good path to get there.” He went on to talk about running the operation. What was Garboden supposed to do when the catering truck was late and the choice was a delayed departure or six hours in first class without meals? In August Garboden began reporting solely to chief commercial officer Nat Pieper and picked up catering, reservations and service recovery. Pieper also got marketing, brand, advertising and partnerships as American broke up Global Engagement head Ron DeFeo’s group. Caroline Clayton took corporate communications. Then I reported network chief Brian Znotins was leaving as Pieper set out to rebuild flying in big cities where American had pulled back. Seymour actually picked up American Eagle in August. But Gulbranson got the airports and operations planning on top of flight operations, flight attendants and the control center. Now he gets safety, regulatory compliance and aircraft maintenance, too. Corporate security goes to government affairs chief Steve Neuman. American will tell employees in December who gets the regionals. If this hadn’t actually been decided already, then August was Gulbranson’s audition. Isom’s memo introduces the retirement as the next step in the August reorganization. Seymour’s contract even lists a material reduction in responsibilities as grounds that can qualify an executive for severance. We don’t know who first proposed retirement, but this looks to me like a negotiated handoff that was already well underway. American Had To Retrofit Planes It Had Just Retrofitted While there are numerous stories like it – such as insufficient oversight of outsourced Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul – I always think of a few things about Seymour’s tenure. One is explaining why the airline wouldn’t invest in RFID baggage tags like Delta despite perpetually bottom of the industry performance in mishandled bags. Another is failing to fix ‘Concept D’ business class seats that rocked. And the biggest is mismanaging cabin retrofits of the domestic fleet. Seymour was running integrated operations when the first American Airlines 737 MAX introduced the cabin that would go into its existing 737s and Airbus A321s. A flight attendant eventually asked whether anyone had built a mockup before committing to it. They hadn’t. Doug Parker said network planning had largely driven the design. Seymour called it “a mistake that should not have happened” and later explained what American had changed. For subsequent cabins they’d bring in real seats, build overhead bins and try pushing a service cart through. In his words, “We do mockups and not just you know ‘tape it out.’” Flight attendants working in the back galley had to help passengers get out of the lavatories because the two doors opened into each other and caught. The sinks were too shallow for the water pressure. I washed my hands on the inaugural flight and got water all over my shirt and pants, as did everyone else. Up front, the seat supports took up the space where a first class passenger was supposed to put a bag. American was still installing the interior after deciding to fix it. Project Oasis put the new seats into existing 737s. Then Project Kodiak went back into planes they’d already redone to fix the storage, give the first row some legroom back and add the device holders coach passengers already had. How Well Did American Actually Run? After the troubled summer of 2019, American gave Seymour responsibility for all operations. The following June he got the chief operating officer title and added flight service. For years my frustration was that when the operation fell short, the answer seemed to be to give the executive running it a bigger job. In 2023 American completed its highest share of scheduled flights since the merger and edged out United on domestic on-time arrivals. And spreading the Dallas schedule from nine daily rushes to 13 smaller ones helped passengers this year. The hub chief reported half as many missed connections in the first 17 days. But by 2025 American ranked eighth of ten network airlines for on-time arrivals. And the Transportation Department’s new figures show that Delta and United both beat American every single month from January through September 2026. Counting domestic flights including regional partners, American came in at 73.30% on time, United at 76.20% and Delta at 78.31%. American canceled 46,059 flights, or 2.99% of its schedule, against 1.75% at United and 2.25% at Delta. Credit: American Airlines One clue to what management valued is in that same proxy. In August 2025 the board gave Seymour a retention stock award worth about $2 million at target. The entire award turns on avoiding cancellations American counts as controllable. A flight that runs three hours late still counts as a success on that measure. The award measures performance through June 2027, so it can still pay out after he’s gone. Gulbranson is well regarded inside American. He started at Northwest, joined US Airways in 2008 and helped integrate flight operations systems during the merger. He’s run both the control center that decides what to cancel and the customer care operation that hears from the people who get stranded. Credit: American Airlines Listen to the two men describe January’s Winter Storm Fern. Seymour said the technology worked as intended and that he hadn’t seen reports of flight attendants sleeping in airports even as his boss Isom acknowledged crew had slept on floors. Gulbranson went before the pilots’ union board and told them where management had misjudged the storm and overestimated how quickly they could recover. The union’s account called his assessment “unvarnished.” That’s one reason I’m glad he’ll be running the operation the next time it snows in Dallas and up the East Coast. His contract calculates severance using pay immediately before termination. Seymour has to sign a release and honor his existing restrictions, and American says it’ll file the full transition letter with its annual report.

Those flight benefits include lifetime confirmed personal travel in any cabin for Seymour and his immediate family, Admirals Club access and another 12 confirmed roundtrips a year for friends and other relatives.

When American put Heather Garboden in charge of the customer experience, they gave her two bosses. She was supposed to persuade customers to pay more to fly American while reporting both to commercial and to the executive responsible for getting flights off the gate on time. When a pilot asked Seymour in 2022 what American was doing about poor customer satisfaction, his answer was “I think we’re on a good path to get there.” He went on to talk about running the operation. What was Garboden supposed to do when the catering truck was late and the choice was a delayed departure or six hours in first class without meals? In August Garboden began reporting solely to chief commercial officer Nat Pieper and picked up catering, reservations and service recovery. Pieper also got marketing, brand, advertising and partnerships as American broke up Global Engagement head Ron DeFeo’s group. Caroline Clayton took corporate communications. Then I reported network chief Brian Znotins was leaving as Pieper set out to rebuild flying in big cities where American had pulled back. Seymour actually picked up American Eagle in August. But Gulbranson got the airports and operations planning on top of flight operations, flight attendants and the control center. Now he gets safety, regulatory compliance and aircraft maintenance, too. Corporate security goes to government affairs chief Steve Neuman. American will tell employees in December who gets the regionals. If this hadn’t actually been decided already, then August was Gulbranson’s audition. Isom’s memo introduces the retirement as the next step in the August reorganization. Seymour’s contract even lists a material reduction in responsibilities as grounds that can qualify an executive for severance. We don’t know who first proposed retirement, but this looks to me like a negotiated handoff that was already well underway. American Had To Retrofit Planes It Had Just Retrofitted While there are numerous stories like it – such as insufficient oversight of outsourced Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul – I always think of a few things about Seymour’s tenure. One is explaining why the airline wouldn’t invest in RFID baggage tags like Delta despite perpetually bottom of the industry performance in mishandled bags. Another is failing to fix ‘Concept D’ business class seats that rocked. And the biggest is mismanaging cabin retrofits of the domestic fleet. Seymour was running integrated operations when the first American Airlines 737 MAX introduced the cabin that would go into its existing 737s and Airbus A321s. A flight attendant eventually asked whether anyone had built a mockup before committing to it. They hadn’t. Doug Parker said network planning had largely driven the design. Seymour called it “a mistake that should not have happened” and later explained what American had changed. For subsequent cabins they’d bring in real seats, build overhead bins and try pushing a service cart through. In his words, “We do mockups and not just you know ‘tape it out.’” Flight attendants working in the back galley had to help passengers get out of the lavatories because the two doors opened into each other and caught. The sinks were too shallow for the water pressure. I washed my hands on the inaugural flight and got water all over my shirt and pants, as did everyone else. Up front, the seat supports took up the space where a first class passenger was supposed to put a bag. American was still installing the interior after deciding to fix it. Project Oasis put the new seats into existing 737s. Then Project Kodiak went back into planes they’d already redone to fix the storage, give the first row some legroom back and add the device holders coach passengers already had. How Well Did American Actually Run? After the troubled summer of 2019, American gave Seymour responsibility for all operations. The following June he got the chief operating officer title and added flight service. For years my frustration was that when the operation fell short, the answer seemed to be to give the executive running it a bigger job. In 2023 American completed its highest share of scheduled flights since the merger and edged out United on domestic on-time arrivals. And spreading the Dallas schedule from nine daily rushes to 13 smaller ones helped passengers this year. The hub chief reported half as many missed connections in the first 17 days. But by 2025 American ranked eighth of ten network airlines for on-time arrivals. And the Transportation Department’s new figures show that Delta and United both beat American every single month from January through September 2026. Counting domestic flights including regional partners, American came in at 73.30% on time, United at 76.20% and Delta at 78.31%. American canceled 46,059 flights, or 2.99% of its schedule, against 1.75% at United and 2.25% at Delta. Credit: American Airlines One clue to what management valued is in that same proxy. In August 2025 the board gave Seymour a retention stock award worth about $2 million at target. The entire award turns on avoiding cancellations American counts as controllable. A flight that runs three hours late still counts as a success on that measure. The award measures performance through June 2027, so it can still pay out after he’s gone. Gulbranson is well regarded inside American. He started at Northwest, joined US Airways in 2008 and helped integrate flight operations systems during the merger. He’s run both the control center that decides what to cancel and the customer care operation that hears from the people who get stranded. Credit: American Airlines Listen to the two men describe January’s Winter Storm Fern. Seymour said the technology worked as intended and that he hadn’t seen reports of flight attendants sleeping in airports even as his boss Isom acknowledged crew had slept on floors. Gulbranson went before the pilots’ union board and told them where management had misjudged the storm and overestimated how quickly they could recover. The union’s account called his assessment “unvarnished.” That’s one reason I’m glad he’ll be running the operation the next time it snows in Dallas and up the East Coast. After the troubled summer of 2019, American gave Seymour responsibility for all operations. The following June he got the chief operating officer title and added flight service. For years my frustration was that when the operation fell short, the answer seemed to be to give the executive running it a bigger job.

In 2023 American completed its highest share of scheduled flights since the merger and edged out United on domestic on-time arrivals. And spreading the Dallas schedule from nine daily rushes to 13 smaller ones helped passengers this year. The hub chief reported half as many missed connections in the first 17 days.

But by 2025 American ranked eighth of ten network airlines for on-time arrivals. And the Transportation Department’s new figures show that Delta and United both beat American every single month from January through September 2026. Counting domestic flights including regional partners, American came in at 73.30% on time, United at 76.20% and Delta at 78.31%. American canceled 46,059 flights, or 2.99% of its schedule, against 1.75% at United and 2.25% at Delta.

One clue to what management valued is in that same proxy. In August 2025 the board gave Seymour a retention stock award worth about $2 million at target. The entire award turns on avoiding cancellations American counts as controllable. A flight that runs three hours late still counts as a success on that measure. The award measures performance through June 2027, so it can still pay out after he’s gone.

Gulbranson is well regarded inside American. He started at Northwest, joined US Airways in 2008 and helped integrate flight operations systems during the merger. He’s run both the control center that decides what to cancel and the customer care operation that hears from the people who get stranded.

Listen to the two men describe January’s Winter Storm Fern. Seymour said the technology worked as intended and that he hadn’t seen reports of flight attendants sleeping in airports even as his boss Isom acknowledged crew had slept on floors.

Gulbranson went before the pilots’ union board and told them where management had misjudged the storm and overestimated how quickly they could recover. The union’s account called his assessment “unvarnished.” That’s one reason I’m glad he’ll be running the operation the next time it snows in Dallas and up the East Coast.

Until Isom and his gang of America West misfits are gone this is nothing more than rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic.

AA is finally addressing the chronic issues that have hurt AA and passenger reason for avoiding them.

DFW is a sprawling mess that AA cannot yet manage anywhere near as effectively as DL manages ATL while CLT is overscheduled.

The most recent DOT data, however, shows that AA is operating far closer to UA than it has in the past. AA’s on-time is within a couple percent of UA – both of which are multiple points behind DL which leads the industry in on-time according to the most recent DOT data.

It is UA that has the industry’s worst baggage even though AA is right above them.

The real improvement is in AA’s invol DB performance which is now below industry average. in fact, it is F9 that singularly is below industry average showing how rare invol DBs are on other carriers – and non-existent on DL even though DL has almost 2X more voluntary DBs than AA.

also worth noting that, for the 3rd quarter, DL led the industry in domestic enplanements, taking the lead from AA a year ago. I suspect it is precisely AA’s poor handling of IROPS that cost it the title of being the US’ largest domestic airline.

and for those that still cling to old advertising, WN was the 4th largest US airline based on domestic enplanements in the 3rd quarter.

The root of the continuing problems at AA is the mess Parker (Former CEO) created. Robert Isom is unable to turn things around and should also “resign”. Nat Pieper should be named CEO to return AA to the great airline it once was.

Baggage handlers, maintenance technicians, customer service staff, and others who actually make the airline happen deserve so, so much more, and yet, this guy gets +$2m just to leave… not right. (I get it; he’s just a mercenary. Still, can’t wait for this 2nd Gilded Age to finally be over.)

That’s an excellent severance package for an established, high-level leader. AA treated him right.

Oh, Tim – can’t resist taking a shot a United when the topic is American. Not surprised. Thanks for the “golden oldie” with the baggage rate reference. UDS!

Also funny that, according to your post, a few percentage points between American and United should be seen as essentially equal, while you still elevate Delta higher than either. When, in fact – United is closer to Delta than American is closer to United, so it’s United and Delta that are essentially the same – using your criteria and “logic”.

YTD, On-time, marketing carrier (Jan – Sept, the latest available DOT data): Delta: 78.31% United: 76.20% (2.11% behind Delta) American: 73.30% (2.90% behind United)

So you can officially stop bragging about Delta being better in on-time stats over United.. Based on your logic, United and Delta are doing equally well. And besides, Alaska is beating all three.

Now – for real, independent analysis, and to get back on topic. Here’s why I believe American is showing the Chief Operating Officer the door. Look at the recovery stats after the ground stop last week. This data is from Flightaware. These are mainline only numbers.

Thurs, Nov 12 (day before shutdown… typical small spattering of cancellations, to establish a baseline): American: 2% Delta: 3% Southwest: 0% United: 1%

Friday Nov 13: (day of shutdown) American: 34% Delta: 31% Southwest: 26% United: 34%

Saturday Nov 14 (attempting to recover – note that American is the only one to go UP during recovery) American: 42% Delta: 28% Southwest: 21% United: 26%

Sunday Nov 15 (full recovery just about everywhere except American) American: 24% Delta: 5% Southwest: 4% United: 3%

Monday Nov 16 (back to baseline cancellations, except small spike seen only at American and twice their original baseline) American: 4% Delta: 0% Southwest: 0% United: 1%

I think this was the final straw that convinced management to show him the door. American’s impact DURING the groundstop wasn’t that abnormal, compared to peers. But the RECOVERY clearly was. They need a change, even if only symbolic.

Also, Tim – you are making up things again and calling them “facts”. Your “facts” are not true, as usual. Let’s pick just one:

Looking at FAA aircraft arrival demand charts (fly.faa.gov/aadc) and Charlotte consistently has demand (operations) well below capacity. Look at BOS for contrast – they regularly get much closer to “scheduled to capacity” daily. Also – look at delay data by airport on flightaware. Charlotte rarely shows up, so American is not running more flights in/out than the gate space can handle. Or it’d show up in the delays.

Either way, thanks for the laughs again, Tim. Always funny to read what you post.

JC Gulbranson continues to move up the chain of command at AAL. Truly one of the great mysteries in life. He and Isom should both get fired.

Sounds like they let the person responsible for the backwards business class seats on the original 787’s. With last row in front cabin having their feet in the galley. Keep their job and looked the other way on their failures

As a passenger, CLT certainly feels over scheduled. Bursting at the seams at every corner. Miserable connecting experience, that feels like the worst in the system. I don’t know what the disconnect is, but CLT certainly can’t take more, regardless of what the FAA says.

The meeting was mercifully brief. “David, you’re fired. And because we’re famously generous and we’re not giving our valued AAdvantage elite passengers free first-class upgrades—here is $2,750,625, the tidy little fortune American Airlines made selling those upgrades this month. Try not to spend it all on a farewell cake. Buh-bye, David.”

paul, thank you for providing the on-time data that indeed shows that UA’s on-time % YTD is closer to AA’s than DL’s.

and the baggage problem is UA’s to fix – and will be highlighted until you tell your boss that you are tired of defending UA’s horrible baggage performance. You can’t argue that AA needs to fix its problems but ignore that UA’s ranking in baggage performance is as low as it is.

and the FAA’s definition of whether an airport is overscheduled is vastly different from a passenger or airline’s. CLT handles about 2X as many passengers as the terminals and concourses can comfortably handle – and AA’s operation and customer service suffers as a result.

Short of spending tens of billions of dollars, which they won’t do, AA has to figure out how to make CLT and DFW work better in order to improve their system level operations.

Given that AA runs a more reliable operation at ORD than UA does – and also has far more aircraft w/ free WiFi – UA has indeed shot itself in the foot no matter how much you run to defend your employer.

You’re hitting the bottle pretty early again today.

>>> “thank you for providing the on-time data that indeed shows that UA’s on-time % YTD is closer to AA’s than DL’s.”

Look at the numbers again, and tell me which airline United is closer to – Delta or American. (Hint… “2.11” is smaller than “2.90”)

Delta: 78.31% United: 76.20% (2.11% behind Delta) American: 73.30% (2.90% behind United)

Now, lets take another thing you said (and did a classic “Pivot!”)… if you want to say the TERMINALS in CLT are overcrowded, that’s a different issue. But you said that Charlotte was “overscheduled”. That’s about the number of flights scheduled in, vs. how many the airport can accommodate.

And you’re wrong, because CLT isn’t overscheduled. The only unbiased way to see if actual, independent (real) data supports the claim any airport is “overscheduled” is to look at:

– The number of flights that an airport can support – The number of flights that are scheduled into the airport

That’s shown in the FAA’s airport arrival/demand charts. If there are too many flights, the charts would show it. They don’t. Arrivals remain well under capacity. If they were even just scheduling it at CLOSE to capacity, you’d see it in the associated delays. You don’t. So, you’re wrong.

As for connections “feeling horrible” (Darin said) – that goes with any airport with lots of available connections. It’s an unavoidable, inverse relationship between connection availability and “next gate” convenience. The more available connections for any single airline, the more planes/gates that must be there to provide those connections. So the more real estate the terminals take up. So the potential for longer distances increases. Same can be said for DFW, ATL, ORD, SFO, DEN, PHL, MSP, PHX, MIA, etc. It’s not unique to CLT.

What can American do? Yes, they can rework the schedules to an extent. Banks can be changed to allow more connection time, but that can affect gate availability at outstations. And the longer the connection time you build, the less attractive the itinerary appears – risking losing customers. But American has been doing it poorly lately – thus the needed changes.

This isn’t that hard, Tim – to verify your info before posting.

>>Look at the numbers again, and tell me which airline United is closer to – Delta or American. (Hint… “2.11” is smaller than “2.90”)

Delta: 78.31% United: 76.20% (2.11% behind Delta) American: 73.30% (2.90% behind United)<<

Then there are cancellations. 29% more likely to have your Delta flight cancelled than a UA flight. UA: 1.75% DL: 2.25% AA: 2.99%

We get it — mastering points and miles is no easy feat. You may have seen our guide to getting started with points and miles, but what happens once you're ready to cash those points in for a trip?

Maximizing points and miles to travel luxuriously without breaking the bank doesn’t need to be laborious and time-consuming. In fact, there are various tools available that make it easier to find hotel and flight award availability.

With these tools, you can use your points to travel where you want, when you want and how you want in 2027 (and beyond) without spending hours searching for availability.

Here are 14 of the best apps and websites that make award travel redemptions easier and less stressful.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: The basic plan is free, but you really unlock the best features with a paid membership. Right now, TPG has a special offer: Roame.travel is offering TPG readers 40% off the Friends of Roame Pro membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY," which brings the regular price down to $94 per year (from $156).

When you sign up for a free Roame account, you can search more than 25 airline programs for instant, real-time award availability.

After clicking a flight option, you can see the points required to book, as well as the available transfer partners and recommended credit cards to help you earn the points you need. You can even add your existing credit cards to your virtual wallet to get recommendations.

With a paid membership, you can also track points pricing with route alerts.

As always, we recommend confirming award availability before transferring points.

Related: The complete guide to searching award space on Roame.travel

What it does: Helps travelers find airline award space.

What it costs: There is a free version that alerts you to seat availability on a specific flight, but you can get additional alerts and better search functions with the Basic ($6.99 per month), Premium ($12.99 per month) or Elite ($19.99 per month) membership options. There are discounts if you choose to pay annually.

And there's an ExpertFlyer discount exclusively for TPG readers: New users can get 30% off any annual subscription.

ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures) is a helpful tool for viewing airline schedules, seat maps and flight statuses across more than 400 airlines, as well as award and upgrade availability on select carriers. You can set seat alerts to help snag your preferred seat if it isn't available when you book your flight.

Related: How to use ExpertFlyer alerts to snag a better seat

A free account lets you set one alert at a time, but you will need a Basic, Premium or Elite membership to run an award search. Once you are logged in with a paid account, you can search using the "Awards & Upgrades" tab. When you enter your travel details and select the airline you'd like to fly, you'll see the fare classes that ExpertFlyer can search alongside a description.

When you click the search button at the bottom of the screen, ExpertFlyer presents you with a list of the available flights broken down by date. Once you have the date, flight number and fare class, you can book your flight online or by calling the airline directly. If the flight you're looking to book doesn't have seats available in your preferred fare class, you can set an alert, and ExpertFlyer will email you if a seat is released, taking the legwork out of award searches.

ExpertFlyer's expanded Systemwide Upgrades feature lets American Airlines elite members with systemwide upgrades search availability up to 330 days out across multiple regions. This feature is only available with ExpertFlyer's Elite plan. Basic and Premium members can still search systemwide upgrade space one route at a time through the “Awards & Upgrades” tab.

What it does: Tracks hotel award availability at Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties.

What it costs: Free for basic membership; $3.99 per month for a Gold membership and $7.99 per month for a Platinum membership (though there's a 40% off Thanksgiving promotion if you elect to pay annually).

MaxMyPoint is a website that lets you check award availability for Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties worldwide. It takes the guesswork out of award redemption searches by showing real-time award pricing and availability.

The homepage shows popular properties, but you can filter by hotel brand, location, price and more to narrow down your results. You can also search date-based deals or use the map search feature to search multiple hotels in a single destination.

Once you choose a property, you can view a calendar that displays available points pricing and the lowest cash rate. This allows you to plan your trip around the dates with the best points pricing.

After you select your check-in date, you’ll automatically be redirected to the property’s website to start the booking process. If you can’t find the availability you are looking for, you can register for a free account and set up an alert to receive an email if availability changes.

Paid memberships come with additional features, including more frequent and more detailed alerts.

What it does: Displays award pricing in Google Flights.

What it costs: Free for a standard plan, $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for a Pro plan. If you want to pay annually, there's also a paid option for alerts only, which costs $34.99 per year.

Points Path is a browser extension that displays award pricing alongside cash prices for select airlines in Google Flights. The free version includes points versus cash pricing for Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue and United Airlines.

It also tells you which transferable points can be used with the airlines it supports, as well as when to book at a paid rate or with points. Once you select an itinerary, you can book it directly with the airline using points or cash, as you would with Google Flights.

Related: How to use the Points Path extension to compare cash and award rates in Google Flights

Points Path simplifies the decision of when to use cash or miles to buy airline tickets. Points Path Pro unlocks additional features such as price alerts, access to additional airline programs and customizable points valuations.

The browser extension is compatible with Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave and Arc.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: There is a free version, but for real-time availability, you can purchase a Standard ($10.75 per month) or Premium ($21.67 per month) membership. These discounts are available when you pay annually. Concierge services are available starting at $200 per passenger.

TPG readers get seven months free on Standard Annual membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY7."

Point.me's robust interface searches for award flights across more than 30 loyalty programs and more than 150 airlines.

By entering your itinerary details, Point.me will display award availability, including which transfer partner offers the most value for your buck.

In addition to the free and paid versions, you can book one-on-one sessions with one of Point.me's expert consultants who can assist you with flight bookings, points strategies, elite status and mileage runs and more.

American Express cardholders can access a limited version of Point.me for free. As with the full version, you can search for award flight availability, but you will only see results from Amex transfer partners. This is a good way to try Point.me for free if you have Membership Rewards points that you want to transfer to an airline loyalty program to purchase tickets.

What it does: Helps you maximize your points by finding the best flight redemptions.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $99 per year for the premium plan (but there's a current promotion for $20 off).

Pointhound takes the guesswork (and hours of searching) out of turning your points and miles into award flights. The site’s search tool helps you find the best deals by displaying preferred booking options for a designated route and date.

For example, if you search for a flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Pointhound will display your flight results alongside all available booking options.

If you know you want to fly Air France but don’t have enough Flying Blue miles, you can see which programs transfer to Air France partners, including those that have current transfer bonuses.

Once you’ve chosen a route and booking option, Pointhound will walk you through the points transfer and booking process. (You still book directly through the airline; Pointhound gives you the instructions on how to do it.)

If you want to stay informed about the latest flight deals, you can sign up to receive flight alerts from specific airports via email.

What it does: Searches for real-time award flight and hotel availability.

What it costs: Free for unlimited basic searches, $19.99 per month or $119.95 per year for Premium (though there are Black Friday promotions).

PointsYeah streamlines hotel and airline award bookings by searching all major credit cards, award programs and booking portals in under 20 seconds. You can view results from more than 20 airline programs and six major hotel programs.

Once you've chosen a flight, PointsYeah will display all available booking options. If you already have enough points, you can book directly with the airline; however, PointsYeah will show the amount of points you'd need to transfer from various credit card programs, including details on current transfer bonuses.

You can create flight and hotel alerts. Basic accounts get up to four flight and hotel price alerts, as well as five multi-region alerts for a 30-day search window.

Premium members get up to 32 flight alerts, 30 hotel alerts and up to 150 multi-region alerts for a 90-day search window. When you upgrade to Premium, you also get access to United Airlines upgrade alerts, expanded date and destination availability when you search and the ability to set custom values for your points currencies.

What it does: Provides real-time search results across multiple airports and travel dates simultaneously.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $12.99 per month or $109.99 per year for AwardTool Pro (with Black Friday discounts available).

If your travel dates and destinations are flexible, AwardTool can display results for multiple flights in a single search. If you're extra flexible, you can utilize the Panorama feature to view award pricing by region rather than a specific destination or the Deals feature to see the best award rates from your chosen airport to anywhere in the world.

When you upgrade to AwardTool Pro, you unlock access to additional and expanded search capabilities, up to 100 award alerts, unlimited Panorama alerts and live seat map availability.

What it does: Gondola helps you find the best hotel deals and use your points to book.

Gondola is a free AI-powered hotel booking tool that tracks your points and miles balances to help you maximize your rewards. When you search for your travel dates and destination, the results will display cash and points pricing, along with ratings to help you determine which is the better value.

You'll see results from major hotel groups like Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Accor and more.

Once you've chosen a property, Gondola will direct you to the hotel's website to book award stays directly with the hotel. For paid reservations, Gondola will book the hotel on your behalf, allowing you to earn the usual points and elite benefits, along with between 3% and 7% cash back in the form of Gondola Cashback for every stay.

Gondola will also monitor your bookings and alert you if the price drops, so you can rebook at the lower price.

What it does: Checks flight award availability based on your itinerary and preferred airline.

What it costs: Free for five economy award availability searches per day; $3.39 per month for a Premium subscription or $9.99 per month for a First Class subscription, with discounts for annual payments.

SeatSpy is an easy-to-use website that checks award availability across 10 airlines, most of which are not U.S.-based carriers.

Select your airline, departure and end destination airports, then hit “Search” to see availability across the next 12 months.

SeatSpy is free to use if you’re only searching for economy availability. Where the product really shines, however, is in its premium subscriptions.

The entry-level subscription, Premium, allows unlimited searches across all fares and up to four active alerts sent via email, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also includes AwardWallet integration, so you can track how many points you have to redeem.

First Class includes everything in the Premium plan, plus unlimited alerts sent instantly instead of hourly, along with SMS alerts and "experience alerts."

Both subscriptions offer a “Where Can I Go” search feature that shows all destinations with award availability from your departure airport on the travel dates you select.

It may have few features when compared to other services on this list, but in terms of simplicity, it’s a great site — especially if you’re looking at Europe-based airlines.

What it does: Displays award seat availability on domestic and international flights across fare classes.

What it costs: Free for the basic version and $12.99 monthly for the Pro version, which includes Rooms.aero access for hotel award searches.

Seats.aero regularly refreshes award space across dozens of airline programs and provides results for the next month or two.

The Pro version allows you to search up to a year in advance, set up unlimited alerts (whereas free users get only five) and receive SMS notifications when award availability turns up.

Related: How I use Seats.aero every day to find the best airline award availability in seconds

What it does: Displays hotel award availability across several major hotel brands.

What it costs: Free for the basic version; if you want the paid Pro version, you can get it through your Seats.aero membership.

Rooms.aero works similarly to its counterpart, Seats.aero. Users can search seven major hotel programs — Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, World of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, I Prefer Hotel Rewards and Wyndham Rewards — for hotel award availability across certain dates or destinations.

Related: How to use Rooms.aero to find the best hotel award availability

Rooms.aero uses a valuation system to indicate whether you are getting good, average or poor value for your points for a given redemption. You can also filter by points program and the maximum number of points per night. When you choose a hotel, you'll see a calendar view with points and cash rates.

You can also use Rooms.aero to set availability alerts to notify you when a specific hotel or destination has points availability. With a Pro account, you get access to advanced search filters, SMS alerts and more.

What it does: Displays points, miles and cash pricing for flights and hotels.

What it costs: Free for a basic membership; $14.99 for a one-time “Trip Pass” valid for three days; and $12.50 per month (or $150 annually) for a premium membership.

Awayz helps you make the most of your hard-earned points and miles by showing when to redeem points and when to pay cash. You can use the Awayz search tool to find specific flight routes or hotels in specific destinations. Awayz will then display live award availability and cash rates so you can make a side-by-side comparison.

You can use the site’s robust filtering system to display certain hotel chains, transferable award programs and even those that qualify for free night certificates.

For flights, you can filter to see only certain airlines, choose the time of day you’d prefer to travel and even indicate which aircraft type you’d prefer. You can also update your “wallet” with the credit cards and reward balances you currently have, so it can tailor your results further.

Related: How to use Awayz to improve your hotel award searches

A free membership includes five hotel and five airline searches per month. An Awayz Trip Pass (great for one-time planning) includes 50 hotel searches, 50 flight searches and 10 award availability alerts for a one-time fee of $14.99. An Awayz Premium membership includes 500 hotel searches, 100 flight searches and 30 award availability alerts, among other perks.

What it does: Finds flight schedules and prices, with several filtering options, for most major airlines.

Google Flights is your one-stop shop for finding the best flight for your schedule and budget.

You can search flight schedules and pricing across most major airlines and sort results based on price, duration, number of stops, fare class and airlines, among other options. You can also set flight price alerts.

One of the best tools within Google Flights is Google Flights Explore.

Google Flights Explore lets you enter only your departure city, then use the interactive map to choose your destination based on current pricing.

Google Flights does not display points pricing (unless you use the Points Path plugin we mentioned earlier in this article), but that doesn’t mean it can’t help you find award space. You’ll still have to book directly through the airline, but you can save valuable search time by narrowing down your options through Google Flights first.

For example, if you have a bank of points and miles with a Star Alliance, Oneworld or SkyTeam partner airline, you can filter search results by alliance to see routing options. Or, you may find a nearby airport with better pricing that you wouldn’t have searched for otherwise.

The great thing about all these tools is that you can use them together to find award flights and free hotel nights.

No matter which combination of sites and apps you use, you’ll find that they take the guesswork out of award redemptions and put you on the fast track to becoming an expert in redeeming points and miles for your 2027 travels.

#6177. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

#6176. Denver Airport’s $225,000 Lawyer Has Been Paid To Stay Home For 8 Months—The City Wants Permission To Fire Him

Denver airport’s top lawyer has spent eight months on paid leave, collecting a salary of roughly $225,000 a year. Now Denver wants a federal judge to let it fire him. But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez says city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job. Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer. I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other. The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting. The distinction between airport money and city money matters here. His salary is airport money. Martinez’s complaint says it comes entirely from the airport’s enterprise fund. That’s separate from Denver’s general fund. Airport revenue consists of things like airline rents and landing fees, parking and concession. That’s not money that can get moved to the city’s programs anyway. The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport. The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage. The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last. Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations. The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year. Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk. Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to). But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. And while he ostensibly also helped protect then-airport CEO Phil Washington, it’s not at all clear that Washington was doing a good job. (He retired August 1.) I covered Washington’s nomination to lead the Federal Aviation Administration and its collapse. He’d spent less than two years running an airport after a career in the military and public transit. During his confirmation hearing, he couldn’t answer a series of seven aviation questions from Senator Ted Budd. And his actual airport record is spotty. Construction oversight. A 2023 audit of the Great Hall project identified inadequate contractor oversight, procurement concerns and overcharges. The January 2025 follow-up found only two of ten recommendations for improvement fully implemented, and no corrective action on seven items. The construction debacle predated Washington, but I view his record as overall quite bad on accountability. Concession revenue. After an audit found weaknesses in rent collection and monitoring concessionaire deductions, the airport accepted 13 recommendations. By October 2025, only three were fully implemented. Accounting problems continued. Executive travel. I wrote about the extraordinary airfare bills for a Madrid conference. The ethics board’s written decision lists $12,047.01 for Washington’s airfare and $19,194.21 for his chief operating officer. My hunch is they were running for MileagePlus status. The board dismissed the ethics complaint for insufficient evidence of private gain, while sharply criticizing the spending and Washington’s response. His ‘need to be ready-to-work-on-arrival’ justification looked weak when he arrived three days before being on the program. The trains remain a good illustration of the airport’s deeper problem. I covered 131 breakdowns over a year. Most interruptions were brief. But passengers still lack a walking alternative to the B and C concourses. Denver is finally planning pedestrian routes through existing baggage tunnels, estimated at $300 million to $700 million, with completion expected in 2028 or 2029. That’s where I’d like to see the airport’s management attention go. Instead, airport users are paying a sidelined general counsel, city taxpayers are funding the defense against him, and the people responsible for running the place are arguing over whether their own lawyer can be trusted. Topics on this pageDenverDenver International AirportEverett MartinezPhil WashingtonFAAMadridMileagePlusSupreme Court of the United States+4 more More From View from the Wing

But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez says city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job.

Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer.

I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other.

The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting.

The distinction between airport money and city money matters here.

The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport.

The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage.

The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last.

Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations.

The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year.

Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk.

Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to).

But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. And while he ostensibly also helped protect then-airport CEO Phil Washington, it’s not at all clear that Washington was doing a good job. (He retired August 1.) #6175. Can Trump’s Agenda Survive the Blue Tsunami?

The core question is whether Republicans can preserve institutional gains long enough for them to become permanent.

President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., November 9, 2026.

The catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term. As I wrote before the election, many aspects of this administration are clearly good from the conservative perspective, not just by comparison to the Biden administration, but to Trump’s own first term and previous Republican administrations since the days of Ronald Reagan.

The border has been secured, deportations have been carried out at a high rate, federal agencies have been forced to abandon much of their institutional commitment to DEI and financial support of the left-wing NGO complex, universities have been put on notice that federal funding is not unconditional, and the administrative state has undergone its most serious shake-up in generations.

President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., November 9, 2026.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

#6174. Trump Says His Private Pilot Used To Use Foreign Air Traffic Control Because The American System Is So Bad

Donald Trump says his private pilot used another country’s air traffic control because the American system was so bad. He wouldn’t identify the country, as though his pilot had discovered a better provider for approaches into Teterboro and didn’t want everyone else signing up. Pilots don’t get that choice. And this isn’t just an ambiguous reference to flying overseas. Trump has made this claim before and described landing in New York, Florida and Tennessee. At his Friday press conference, Trump said his “pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country.” This was supposedly before his first term, 11 or 12 years ago. Then he declared, “I know a lot about air traffic control.” Watch Trump describe his pilot using another country’s air traffic control — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar), November 20, 2026 Air traffic control assigns clearances and separates aircraft sharing the same airspace. The controller responsible for your flight changes as you move between sectors and facilities. Your pilot can request a different route or altitude. They can reject an unsafe instruction. They can’t decide to use a different country’s air traffic control service because they like it better. And there’s a clear division of responsibilities. Pilots fly the aircraft and request changes to clearances when needed. Controllers coordinate the traffic. Could There Be A Real Story Behind This? I’ve tried to come up with something plausible, to create the most generous interpretation of these remarks. The best I can do is that Trump is confusing navigation equipment with air traffic control. Perhaps his pilot told him about a preferred navigation system, approach procedure or a piece of equipment he liked from overseas, and that became a story about choosing another country’s controllers. There are also real circumstances where an American flight uses foreign air traffic services: Crossing the North Atlantic. A flight to Scotland could pass through airspace handled by Nav Canada’s Gander operation and Britain’s Shanwick operation. Taking a route through Canada. A pilot could request a route that avoids congested U.S. sectors and spends more time in Canadian airspace (but it doesn’t give Canadian controllers responsibility for a landing in Tennessee). Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller. None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025. So, if I’m landing in New York or Florida or Tennessee, they’re using a system from another country. He repeated the story on June 27, 2025, too. So this is a recurring explanation of how he thinks flying works. The U.S. System Really Does Need Fixing I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country. I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years. In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service. This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President. I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country.

I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years.

In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service.

This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President.

#6173. Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure update: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He said the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for New Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism.
